claim: The budding yeast centromere contains Cse4, a specialized histone H3 variant.
source: The budding yeast centromere contains Cse4, a specialized histone H3 variant.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about yeast centromeres.

claim: Internally tagged Cse4 is replaced with newly synthesized molecules in S phase.
source: Fluorescence pulse-chase analysis of an internally tagged Cse4 reveals that it is replaced with newly synthesized molecules in S phase, remaining stably associated with centromeres thereafter.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence pulse-chase experiments described in the abstract and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Internally tagged Cse4 remains stably associated with centromeres after S phase replacement.
source: Fluorescence pulse-chase analysis of an internally tagged Cse4 reveals that it is replaced with newly synthesized molecules in S phase, remaining stably associated with centromeres thereafter.
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments tracking Cse4-tdEos through the cell cycle.

claim: C-terminally-tagged Cse4 is functionally impaired.
source: In contrast, C-terminally-tagged Cse4 is functionally impaired, showing slow cell growth, cell lethality at elevated temperatures, and extra-centromeric nuclear accumulation.
evidence: Demonstrated by growth assays and microscopy shown in Figure 1.

claim: C-terminally-tagged Cse4 shows slow cell growth.
source: In contrast, C-terminally-tagged Cse4 is functionally impaired, showing slow cell growth, cell lethality at elevated temperatures, and extra-centromeric nuclear accumulation.
evidence: Shown in viability tests in Figure 1F.

claim: C-terminally-tagged Cse4 shows cell lethality at elevated temperatures.
source: In contrast, C-terminally-tagged Cse4 is functionally impaired, showing slow cell growth, cell lethality at elevated temperatures, and extra-centromeric nuclear accumulation.
evidence: Demonstrated by temperature sensitivity assays in Figure 1F.

claim: C-terminally-tagged Cse4 shows extra-centromeric nuclear accumulation.
source: In contrast, C-terminally-tagged Cse4 is functionally impaired, showing slow cell growth, cell lethality at elevated temperatures, and extra-centromeric nuclear accumulation.
evidence: Shown by fluorescence microscopy in Figure 1E.

claim: Internally tagged Cse4 is a better reporter of the biology of this histone variant than C-terminally tagged Cse4.
source: Our findings indicate that internally tagged Cse4 is a better reporter of the biology of this histone variant.
evidence: Based on comparison of functional properties between internal and C-terminal tags.

claim: Centromeric Cse4 clusters undergo substantial compaction during anaphase.
source: Furthermore, the size of centromeric Cse4 clusters was precisely mapped with a new 3D-PALM method, revealing substantial compaction during anaphase.
evidence: Demonstrated by 3D-PALM measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: Scm3 displays steady-state, stoichiometric co-localization with Cse4 at centromeres throughout the cell cycle.
source: Cse4-specific chaperone Scm3 displays steady-state, stoichiometric co-localization with Cse4 at centromeres throughout the cell cycle, while undergoing exchange with a nuclear pool.
evidence: Shown by fluorescence microscopy and photobleaching experiments in Figure 8.

claim: Scm3 undergoes exchange with a nuclear pool.
source: Cse4-specific chaperone Scm3 displays steady-state, stoichiometric co-localization with Cse4 at centromeres throughout the cell cycle, while undergoing exchange with a nuclear pool.
evidence: Demonstrated by targeted photobleaching and recovery experiments in Figure 8.

claim: A stable Cse4 nucleosome is maintained by dynamic chaperone-in-residence Scm3.
source: These findings suggest that a stable Cse4 nucleosome is maintained by dynamic chaperone-in-residence Scm3.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of Cse4 stability and Scm3 dynamics data.

claim: Accurate segregation of genetic material constitutes the basis of cell division and inheritance in all eukaryotes.
source: In all eukaryotes, accurate segregation of genetic material constitutes the basis of cell division and inheritance.
evidence: This is established biological knowledge.

claim: Chromosome segregation is controlled by a complex signalling network targeting the kinetochore.
source: Chromosome segregation is controlled by a complex signalling network targeting the kinetochore—a protein superstructure of some 100 polypeptides, anchoring chromosomes to the mitotic spindle through interaction with a specialized region of the chromosome, the centromere.
evidence: This is established biological knowledge.

claim: The kinetochore is a protein superstructure of some 100 polypeptides.
source: Chromosome segregation is controlled by a complex signalling network targeting the kinetochore—a protein superstructure of some 100 polypeptides, anchoring chromosomes to the mitotic spindle through interaction with a specialized region of the chromosome, the centromere.
evidence: This is established biological knowledge.

claim: The kinetochore anchors chromosomes to the mitotic spindle through interaction with the centromere.
source: Chromosome segregation is controlled by a complex signalling network targeting the kinetochore—a protein superstructure of some 100 polypeptides, anchoring chromosomes to the mitotic spindle through interaction with a specialized region of the chromosome, the centromere.
evidence: This is established biological knowledge.

claim: The chromatin structure of centromeres is distinguished by nucleosomes containing a distinct variant of histone H3, called CENP-A or CenH3.
source: The chromatin structure of centromeres is distinguished from other chromosome regions by nucleosomes containing a distinct variant of histone H3, called CENP-A or CenH3 (Biggins, 2013; Westhorpe and Straight, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The centromere of Saccharomyces cerevisiae is fully specified by a short DNA segment of approximately 125 bp.
source: Unlike other organisms, in which centromeres encompass extended regions with tens or thousands of CENP-A nucleosomes, the centromere of the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae is fully specified by a short DNA segment (CEN, ∼125 bp) (Gaudet and Fitzgerald–Hayes, 1987; Murphy et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The budding yeast 'point' centromere consists of a single nucleosome-like chromatin particle containing Cse4.
source: This so-called 'point' centromere consists of a single nucleosome-like chromatin particle containing Cse4, the yeast ortholog of CENP-A (Stoler et al., 1995; Meluh et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cse4 is the yeast ortholog of CENP-A.
source: This so-called 'point' centromere consists of a single nucleosome-like chromatin particle containing Cse4, the yeast ortholog of CENP-A (Stoler et al., 1995; Meluh et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Three contiguous centromeric DNA elements CDEI, CDE II, and CDE III direct assembly of a Cse4 nucleosome.
source: Classic genetic, molecular, and biochemical studies have defined three contiguous centromeric DNA elements CDEI, CDE II, and CDE III that direct assembly of a Cse4 nucleosome by sequence-specific DNA binding factors CBF1 and CBF3 (Cai and Davis, 1990; Lechner and Carbon, 1991) and Scm3, a Cse4-specific chaperone (Camahort et al., 2007; Mizuguchi et al., 2007; Stoler et al., 2007; Xiao et al., 2011; Cho and Harrison, 2011b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CBF1 and CBF3 are sequence-specific DNA binding factors that direct assembly of a Cse4 nucleosome.
source: Classic genetic, molecular, and biochemical studies have defined three contiguous centromeric DNA elements CDEI, CDE II, and CDE III that direct assembly of a Cse4 nucleosome by sequence-specific DNA binding factors CBF1 and CBF3 (Cai and Davis, 1990; Lechner and Carbon, 1991) and Scm3, a Cse4-specific chaperone (Camahort et al., 2007; Mizuguchi et al., 2007; Stoler et al., 2007; Xiao et al., 2011; Cho and Harrison, 2011b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Scm3 is a Cse4-specific chaperone that directs assembly of a Cse4 nucleosome.
source: Classic genetic, molecular, and biochemical studies have defined three contiguous centromeric DNA elements CDEI, CDE II, and CDE III that direct assembly of a Cse4 nucleosome by sequence-specific DNA binding factors CBF1 and CBF3 (Cai and Davis, 1990; Lechner and Carbon, 1991) and Scm3, a Cse4-specific chaperone (Camahort et al., 2007; Mizuguchi et al., 2007; Stoler et al., 2007; Xiao et al., 2011; Cho and Harrison, 2011b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cse4 nucleosomes have been reported to contain chaperone Scm3 and dislocated histones H2A-H2B.
source: Cse4 nucleosomes have been reported to differ from the canonical nucleosome not only by the replacement of both molecules of histone H3 by the Cse4 variant, but also by the presence of chaperone Scm3 and dislocation of histones H2A-H2B (Mizuguchi et al., 2007; Xiao et al., 2011), or by existence of a hemisome particle bearing half the histone content (Dalal et al., 2007; Furuyama et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cse4 nucleosomes have been reported to exist as a hemisome particle bearing half the histone content.
source: Cse4 nucleosomes have been reported to differ from the canonical nucleosome not only by the replacement of both molecules of histone H3 by the Cse4 variant, but also by the presence of chaperone Scm3 and dislocation of histones H2A-H2B (Mizuguchi et al., 2007; Xiao et al., 2011), or by existence of a hemisome particle bearing half the histone content (Dalal et al., 2007; Furuyama et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Live cell microscopy of GFP-tagged Cse4 has indicated that the number of Cse4 molecules associated with centromeres may be several-fold greater than two.
source: Moreover, live cell microscopy of GFP-tagged Cse4 have variously indicated that the number of Cse4 molecules associated with centromeres may be either several-fold greater than the two Cse4 molecules within a nucleosome (Coffman et al., 2011; Lawrimore et al., 2011), or oscillate during mitosis from one to two molecules per centromeric nucleosome (Shivaraju et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Live cell microscopy of GFP-tagged Cse4 has indicated that the number of Cse4 molecules may oscillate during mitosis from one to two molecules per centromeric nucleosome.
source: Moreover, live cell microscopy of GFP-tagged Cse4 have variously indicated that the number of Cse4 molecules associated with centromeres may be either several-fold greater than the two Cse4 molecules within a nucleosome (Coffman et al., 2011; Lawrimore et al., 2011), or oscillate during mitosis from one to two molecules per centromeric nucleosome (Shivaraju et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Insertions or deletions within the N-terminal tail of Cse4 do not impose any deleterious growth phenotype as long as the 33-residue essential END domain is preserved.
source: These workers showed that insertions or deletions within the N-terminal tail do not impose any deleterious growth phenotype at all tested temperatures, as long as a 33-residue essential END domain, that interacts with the Ctf19-Mcm21-Okp1 kinetochore sub-complex, is preserved.
evidence: Based on previous studies by Stoler et al. (1995) and Chen et al. (2000).

claim: The END domain of Cse4 interacts with the Ctf19-Mcm21-Okp1 kinetochore sub-complex.
source: These workers showed that insertions or deletions within the N-terminal tail do not impose any deleterious growth phenotype at all tested temperatures, as long as a 33-residue essential END domain, that interacts with the Ctf19-Mcm21-Okp1 kinetochore sub-complex, is preserved.
evidence: Based on previous studies.

claim: The extreme C-terminal residues of Cse4 (QFI, aa 227-229) mediate recognition by CENP-C.
source: In contrast, the extreme C-terminal residues of Cse4 (QFI, aa 227-229, located close to the structured part of the nucleosome [Tachiwana et al., 2011]) mediate recognition by CENP-C (Kato et al., 2013) and an adjoining tag is likely to impair this interaction.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kato et al., 2013.

claim: A C-terminal tag on Cse4 is likely to impair interaction with CENP-C.
source: In contrast, the extreme C-terminal residues of Cse4 (QFI, aa 227-229, located close to the structured part of the nucleosome [Tachiwana et al., 2011]) mediate recognition by CENP-C (Kato et al., 2013) and an adjoining tag is likely to impair this interaction.
evidence: Inferred from the location of the C-terminal tag relative to the CENP-C interaction site.

claim: Functionality of Drosophila CENP-A/CenH3 is preserved by an internal insertion of GFP but not by a C-terminal fusion.
source: Moreover, functionality of Drosophila CENP-A/CenH3 is also preserved by an internal insertion of GFP but not by a C-terminal fusion (Schuh et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schuh et al., 2007.

claim: Internally tagged Cse4-GFP reveals fluorescence exclusively in a single dot or a pair of dots corresponding to clusters of yeast centromeres.
source: Live cell imaging of internally tagged Cse4-GFP reveals fluorescence exclusively in a single dot or a pair of dots (Figure 1C), corresponding to the clusters of yeast centromeres (Jin et al., 1998; Meluh et al., 1998; Chen et al., 2000; Jin et al., 2000).
evidence: Shown by microscopy in Figure 1C and supported by citations.

claim: Internal Cse4-tdEos fusion shows identical localization results to Cse4-GFP despite the larger tag size.
source: Identical results are obtained for internal Cse4-tdEos fusion, despite the larger tag size (Figure 1D).
evidence: Shown by microscopy in Figure 1D.

claim: S phase centromeres display weaker tdEos fluorescence.
source: Curiously, S phase centromeres display weaker tdEos fluorescence (Figure 1D), a phenomenon further explored below.
evidence: Observed in microscopy images in Figure 1D.

claim: C-terminally tagged Cse4-GFP shows extra-centromeric fluorescence throughout nuclei at every stage of the cell cycle.
source: However, in contrast to internally tagged Cse4, we clearly detect extra-centromeric fluorescence throughout nuclei at every stage of the cell cycle (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown by microscopy in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: C-terminal Cse4-GFP is present at approximately twofold excess compared to internal Cse4-GFP fusion.
source: This difference is confirmed by Western blot analysis of whole cell extracts, showing ∼twofold excess of C-terminal over internal Cse4-GFP fusion of comparable size and blotting efficiency (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), while internally tagged Cse4 is present at levels close to wild-type Cse4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–G).
evidence: Shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Internally tagged Cse4 is present at levels close to wild-type Cse4.
source: This difference is confirmed by Western blot analysis of whole cell extracts, showing ∼twofold excess of C-terminal over internal Cse4-GFP fusion of comparable size and blotting efficiency (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), while internally tagged Cse4 is present at levels close to wild-type Cse4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–G).
evidence: Shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–G.

claim: The C-terminal Cse4-GFP strain exhibits slow growth in rich medium even at 24°C.
source: The C-terminal Cse4-GFP strain exhibits slow growth in rich medium even at 24°C, and is not viable at 38°C, while none of the internal fusions have growth defects at either temperature (Figure 1F).
evidence: Shown by viability tests in Figure 1F.

claim: The C-terminal Cse4-GFP strain is not viable at 38°C.
source: The C-terminal Cse4-GFP strain exhibits slow growth in rich medium even at 24°C, and is not viable at 38°C, while none of the internal fusions have growth defects at either temperature (Figure 1F).
evidence: Shown by viability tests in Figure 1F.

claim: None of the internal Cse4 fusions have growth defects at 24°C or 38°C.
source: The C-terminal Cse4-GFP strain exhibits slow growth in rich medium even at 24°C, and is not viable at 38°C, while none of the internal fusions have growth defects at either temperature (Figure 1F).
evidence: Shown by viability tests in Figure 1F.

claim: Fusion of a fluorescent protein tag to the C-terminus impairs Cse4 function.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that fusion of a fluorescent protein tag to the C-terminus impairs Cse4 function.
evidence: Concluded from growth and localization data.

claim: tdEos fluorophores undergo relatively slow maturation to a green fluorescent state after synthesis and protein folding.
source: After synthesis and protein folding, tdEos fluorophores undergo relatively slow maturation to a green fluorescent state (Nienhaus et al., 2006) (Figure 2A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation and shown in Figure 2A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Upon exposure to violet light, mature tdEos fluorophores undergo almost instantaneous, irreversible photoconversion to a red-emitting state.
source: However, upon exposure to violet light, such mature fluorophores undergo almost instantaneous, irreversible photoconversion to a red-emitting state.
evidence: This is a known property of tdEos.

claim: Cells crossing the G1/S boundary lose centromeric fluorescence of pre-existing Cse4.
source: Figure 2D shows that centromeric clusters typically retain pre-existing Cse4, with the striking exception of cells crossing the G1/S boundary (magenta outlines), which lose centromeric fluorescence.
evidence: Shown by pulse-chase experiments in Figure 2D.

claim: Pre-existing Cse4 is not maintained or recycled in S phase.
source: This indicates that pre-existing Cse4 is not maintained or recycled in S phase.
evidence: Inferred from the loss of photoconverted Cse4 signal at G1/S transition.

claim: New Cse4 molecules are loaded at centromeric clusters in S phase.
source: An additional round of photoconversion at the end of the experiment confirms loading of new Cse4 molecules at centromeric clusters (Figure 2E), in accordance with previous studies showing Cse4-GFP deposition in S phase (Pearson et al., 2004; JW, personal communication).
evidence: Shown by second photoconversion in Figure 2E and supported by citations.

claim: Early in S phase, Cse4 molecules are eliminated and replaced by newly synthesized molecules.
source: Taken together, our results document that early in S phase, Cse4 molecules are eliminated and replaced by newly synthesized molecules, thereafter remaining stably associated with centromeres through the rest of the cell cycle.
evidence: Concluded from pulse-chase experiments in Figure 2.

claim: After S phase replacement, Cse4 remains stably associated with centromeres through the rest of the cell cycle.
source: Taken together, our results document that early in S phase, Cse4 molecules are eliminated and replaced by newly synthesized molecules, thereafter remaining stably associated with centromeres through the rest of the cell cycle.
evidence: Concluded from pulse-chase experiments in Figure 2.

claim: There is no persistent pool of free nuclear or cytoplasmic Cse4.
source: The results also indicate the absence of a persistent pool of free nuclear or cytoplasmic Cse4, as we fail to observe carry-through of pre-existing Cse4 into S phase.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of carry-through of pre-existing Cse4 into S phase.

claim: The fluorescence of Cse4 clusters increases gradually from S phase through mitosis for both tdEos and GFP insertions.
source: The fluorescence of Cse4 clusters increases gradually from S phase through mitosis for both tdEos and GFP insertions (Figure 3A).
evidence: Shown by fluorescence measurements in Figure 3A.

claim: The brightness of newly formed centromere clusters increases with time until it reaches a plateau at approximately 70 min when protein synthesis is blocked.
source: We find that their brightness increases with time until it reaches a plateau at ∼70 min, remaining stable for at least 120 min thereafter, notwithstanding the cycloheximide-induced block in cell cycle progression (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Shown by experiments with cycloheximide in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The half-time of tdEos maturation at 25°C is approximately 40 min.
source: This intensity profile indicates that the half-time of maturation at 25°C is approximately 40 min—similar to the time observed for half-maximal increase of Cse4-tdEos fluorescence in a population of asynchronously growing cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Calculated from fluorescence increase data in Figure 3.

claim: Fluorophore maturation is sufficient to explain the gradual rise of Cse4-tdEos fluorescence through the cell cycle after early S phase deposition.
source: Hence, fluorophore maturation is sufficient to explain the gradual rise of Cse4-tdEos fluorescence through the cell cycle after early S phase deposition.
evidence: Concluded from cycloheximide experiments showing fluorescence increase without protein synthesis.

claim: Cells treated with hydroxyurea uniformly retain pre-existing Cse4 on centromere clusters, regardless of bud emergence.
source: However, cells treated with hydroxyurea uniformly retain pre-existing Cse4 on centromere clusters, regardless of bud emergence.
evidence: Shown by pulse-chase experiments with hydroxyurea in Figure 4B.

claim: The removal of old Cse4 from centromeres is associated with DNA replication.
source: This suggests that the removal of old Cse4 from centromeres is associated with DNA replication.
evidence: Inferred from hydroxyurea experiments blocking DNA replication.

claim: Additional Cse4 deposition did not occur on the bleached cluster during anaphase progression.
source: Upon progression through anaphase, we find that only one red-fluorescent cluster is visible at telophase as well (Figure 5B3). This indicates that additional Cse4 deposition did not occur on the bleached cluster, nor did Cse4 exchange between the two clusters.
evidence: Shown by targeted FRAP experiments in Figure 5B.

claim: Cse4 does not exchange between the two centromere clusters during anaphase.
source: Upon progression through anaphase, we find that only one red-fluorescent cluster is visible at telophase as well (Figure 5B3). This indicates that additional Cse4 deposition did not occur on the bleached cluster, nor did Cse4 exchange between the two clusters.
evidence: Shown by targeted FRAP experiments in Figure 5B.

claim: There is compositional stasis for Cse4 after S phase deposition.
source: Hence, our results indicate a compositional stasis for Cse4 after S phase deposition, and do not support a second wave of Cse4 deposition in anaphase.
evidence: Concluded from targeted FRAP experiments.

claim: There is no second wave of Cse4 deposition in anaphase.
source: Hence, our results indicate a compositional stasis for Cse4 after S phase deposition, and do not support a second wave of Cse4 deposition in anaphase.
evidence: Concluded from targeted FRAP experiments.

claim: Cse4 clusters in G1 are typically approximately 450 nm across.
source: We find that Cse4 clusters in G1 are typically ∼450 nm across (Figure 6D,F; Video 2), clearly indicating that their wide-field image (the sum of all individual Airy disks) would significantly exceed the diffraction limit (in this case an Airy disk with FWHM ∼225 nm).
evidence: Measured by MFM-PALM in Figure 6D,F.

claim: Anaphase Cse4 clusters are more compact and asymmetric, on average approximating an ellipsoid of 350 nm × 200 nm.
source: Strikingly, anaphase clusters are more compact and asymmetric, on average approximating an ellipsoid of 350 nm × 200 nm (still above the diffraction limit—Figure 6E,G; Video 3).
evidence: Measured by MFM-PALM in Figure 6E,G.

claim: The change in Cse4 cluster size from G1 to anaphase corresponds to approximately threefold reduction in volume.
source: This change corresponds to ∼threefold reduction in the volume of the cluster and thus higher spatial density of centromeres.
evidence: Calculated from MFM-PALM measurements.

claim: The shortened polar axis of anaphase clusters frequently coincides with the direction of the mitotic spindle.
source: Frequently, the shortened polar axis coincides with the direction of the mitotic spindle extending between anaphase clusters (Video 1).
evidence: Observed in MFM-PALM data shown in Video 1.

claim: Median intensity of wavelet filtered Cse4-GFP clusters corresponds to approximately 36 GFP molecules.
source: Figure 7B shows that median intensity of wavelet filtered Cse4-GFP clusters corresponds to ∼36 GFP molecules.
evidence: Measured by photometry in Figure 7B.

claim: The median intensity of Cse4-GFP clusters is consistent with two Cse4 molecules for each of the 16 centromeres clustered together in telophase.
source: Given the scatter of measured values, this is consistent with two Cse4 molecules for each of the 16 centromeres clustered together in telophase.
evidence: Inferred from photometry measurements compared to tetO arrays.

claim: There is approximately fourfold excess of free Scm3-tdEos throughout the nucleus compared to the centromeric-bound protein.
source: Comparison of total nuclear and centromeric fluorescence reveals ∼fourfold excess of free Scm3-tdEos throughout the nucleus compared to the centromeric-bound protein (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Measured by fluorescence microscopy in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Scm3 undergoes exchange between centromeres and the free nuclear pool.
source: In contrast to the stability of Cse4-tdEos, Scm3 fluorescence reappears on the cluster within several minutes (between 4 and 11 min in this example), demonstrating that, unlike Cse4, Scm3 undergoes exchange between centromeres and the free nuclear pool.
evidence: Shown by targeted photobleaching experiments in Figure 8A.

claim: The average recovery time of Scm3 at centromeres is approximately 5 min throughout the cell cycle.
source: When measured throughout the cell cycle, the average recovery time (at which fluorescence is detected again) is ∼5 min (Table 1).
evidence: Measured by targeted photobleaching experiments shown in Table 1.

claim: Dynamic exchange of Scm3 with persistent, steady-state occupancy may ensure continuing integrity of the singular centromeric nucleosome after Cse4 deposition in S phase.
source: Such dynamic exchange of Scm3 with persistent, steady-state occupancy may ensure continuing integrity of the singular centromeric nucleosome after Cse4 deposition in S phase.
evidence: Speculated based on Scm3 dynamics data.

claim: Total pre-existing Scm3 persists through multiple cell cycles, with gradual dilution during consecutive cell divisions.
source: A pulse-chase experiment shows that total pre-existing Scm3 persists through multiple cell cycles, with gradual dilution during consecutive cell divisions, indicating its low rate of turn-over (Figure 8B).
evidence: Shown by pulse-chase experiments in Figure 8B.

claim: Steady-state fluorescence of centromeric Scm3 shows a mild decrease in S phase.
source: Moreover, steady-state fluorescence of centromeric Scm3 shows a mild decrease in S phase, suggesting synthesis of new Scm3 molecules with immature fluorophores during that stage (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Observed in microscopy data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Near equimolar levels of Scm3 and Cse4 coexist on centromere clusters throughout the cell cycle.
source: Taking into account that Cse4 remains stable after deposition and Scm3 interacts dynamically and persistently with centromeres, this indicates that near equimolar levels of both proteins coexist on centromere clusters throughout the cell cycle.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of Scm3 and Cse4 fluorescence intensities.

claim: A C-terminal GFP tag impairs Cse4 functionality, causing severe growth defects and substantial extra-centromeric accumulation.
source: In a side-by-side comparison, we document that a C-terminal GFP tag impairs Cse4 functionality, causing severe growth defects and substantial extra-centromeric accumulation.
evidence: Demonstrated by growth assays and microscopy.

claim: A C-terminal FLAG epitope tag on Cse4 causes similar growth defects to C-terminal GFP.
source: We observed similar growth defects with a FLAG epitope tag as well (GM, unpublished data).
evidence: Mentioned as unpublished observation.

claim: The extreme C-terminal residues of Cse4 specify recognition by Mif2, the yeast CENP-C inner kinetochore protein.
source: The extreme C-terminal residues of Cse4 specify recognition by Mif2, the yeast CENP-C inner kinetochore protein (Kato et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kato et al., 2013.

claim: A C-terminal fusion is likely to affect interaction with Mif2, perturbing kinetochore functionality.
source: Accordingly, a C-terminal fusion is likely to affect such interaction, perturbing kinetochore functionality.
evidence: Inferred from the location of the C-terminal tag relative to the Mif2 interaction site.

claim: The molecular phenotypes of C-terminally tagged Cse4-GFP reflect properties of functionally impaired Cse4, rather than the native protein.
source: Thus, the molecular phenotypes of C-terminally tagged Cse4-GFP reflect properties of functionally impaired Cse4, rather than the native protein.
evidence: Concluded from comparison of C-terminal and internal tags.

claim: Partial loss of function was observed for C-terminally tagged CENP-A/CenH3 in mouse.
source: Similarly, partial loss of function was also observed for C-terminally tagged CENP-A/CenH3 in mouse (Kalitsis et al., 2003) and Drosophila (Schuh et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations.

claim: Partial loss of function was observed for C-terminally tagged CENP-A/CenH3 in Drosophila.
source: Similarly, partial loss of function was also observed for C-terminally tagged CENP-A/CenH3 in mouse (Kalitsis et al., 2003) and Drosophila (Schuh et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations.

claim: Internally tagged Cse4 fusions should be used in imaging studies as a preferred reporter of the composition and dynamics of centromeric nucleosomes.
source: Thus, internally tagged Cse4 fusions should be used in imaging studies as a preferred reporter of the composition and dynamics of centromeric nucleosomes.
evidence: Recommended based on comparison of internal and C-terminal tags.

claim: The internal photoconvertible tdEos tag minimizes autofluorescence and improves signal to noise.
source: The internal photoconvertible tdEos tag allows a direct analysis of Cse4 dynamics in live cells, minimizes autofluorescence, improves signal to noise, and enables excitation at low energies to limit phototoxicity and cell cycle perturbation.
evidence: Based on properties of tdEos and experimental observations.

claim: The internal photoconvertible tdEos tag enables excitation at low energies to limit phototoxicity and cell cycle perturbation.
source: The internal photoconvertible tdEos tag allows a direct analysis of Cse4 dynamics in live cells, minimizes autofluorescence, improves signal to noise, and enables excitation at low energies to limit phototoxicity and cell cycle perturbation.
evidence: Based on properties of tdEos.

claim: Cse4 replacement is linked to DNA synthesis.
source: This reveals replacement of Cse4 exclusively in early S phase, linked to DNA synthesis—consistent with the timing of centromere replication (McCarroll and Fangman, 1988; Pohl et al., 2012).
evidence: Demonstrated by hydroxyurea experiments and supported by citations.

claim: The timing of Cse4 replacement is consistent with the timing of centromere replication.
source: This reveals replacement of Cse4 exclusively in early S phase, linked to DNA synthesis—consistent with the timing of centromere replication (McCarroll and Fangman, 1988; Pohl et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations.

claim: The S phase deposition of Cse4 involves removal of pre-existing Cse4 followed by the deposition of newly synthesized molecules, without recycling of old Cse4.
source: Our data elaborate on the S phase deposition of Cse4 reported by Pearson et al. (2004), by showing this process as a removal of pre-existing Cse4 followed by the deposition of newly synthesized molecules, without recycling of old Cse4.
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments.

claim: Budding yeast Cse4 has no epigenetic role in kinetochore inheritance.
source: In this context, budding yeast Cse4 has no epigenetic role in kinetochore inheritance, in contrast to the inheritance of CENP-A on regional centromeres of other organisms (De Rop et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from the complete replacement of Cse4 in S phase.

claim: CENP-A on regional centromeres of other organisms has an epigenetic role in inheritance.
source: In this context, budding yeast Cse4 has no epigenetic role in kinetochore inheritance, in contrast to the inheritance of CENP-A on regional centromeres of other organisms (De Rop et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation.

claim: Interpretation of fluorescence intensities for proteins undergoing synthesis and exchange at a highly specific moment of the cell cycle requires caution.
source: Accordingly, interpretation of fluorescence intensities for proteins undergoing synthesis and exchange at a highly specific moment of the cell cycle requires caution.
evidence: Concluded from observations of fluorophore maturation effects.

claim: Centromere clusters frequently appear more point-like in anaphase and telophase than in G1 in conventional microscopy.
source: Furthermore, in conventional microscopy, centromere clusters frequently appear more point-like in anaphase and telophase than in G1, which may give the impression of a rise in fluorescence when viewed against the increased nuclear background caused by C-terminal Cse4-GFP fusions (Joglekar et al., 2006; Aravamudhan et al., 2013).
evidence: Observed in microscopy and supported by citations.

claim: 3D-PALM provides resolution superior to previous results based on bulk analysis for mapping centromere clusters.
source: A new super-resolution 3D-PALM approach allowed mapping of the actual spatial distribution of individual Cse4 molecules in the centromere cluster, indicating that it should not be treated as a point source for photometric analysis, and providing resolution superior to previous results based on bulk analysis (Haase et al., 2013).
evidence: Demonstrated by 3D-PALM measurements and comparison to previous methods.

claim: Compaction of centromere clusters leads to approximately threefold higher spatial density of centromeres in anaphase.
source: Such compaction of centromere clusters leads to ∼threefold higher spatial density of centromeres, increasing the likelihood that individual Cse4 molecules on separate centromeres come into proximity sufficient for FRET.
evidence: Calculated from 3D-PALM measurements.

claim: Higher spatial density of centromeres in anaphase increases the likelihood that individual Cse4 molecules on separate centromeres come into proximity sufficient for FRET.
source: Such compaction of centromere clusters leads to ∼threefold higher spatial density of centromeres, increasing the likelihood that individual Cse4 molecules on separate centromeres come into proximity sufficient for FRET.
evidence: Inferred from increased spatial density.

claim: Higher FRET efficiency in anaphase may be explained as interactions between centromeres, without the need to invoke structural oscillation of the centromeric nucleosome.
source: This may explain the higher FRET efficiency reported in anaphase (Shivaraju et al., 2012) as interactions between centromeres, without the need to invoke structural oscillation of the centromeric nucleosome between hemisome and octasome.
evidence: Inferred from centromere compaction data and cited FRET observations.

claim: Previous biochemical and molecular genetic evidence led to a model for a single centromeric nucleosome per yeast chromosome, each containing two Cse4 molecules.
source: Previous biochemical and molecular genetic evidence led to a model for a single centromeric nucleosome per yeast chromosome, each containing two Cse4 molecules, located at the ∼125 bp CEN sequence common to all 16 yeast chromosomes (Chen et al., 2000; Smith, 2002; Furuyama and Biggins, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The use of C-terminally tagged Cse4 yielded estimates ranging from 1 to 8 Cse4 molecules per centromere.
source: In contrast, the use of C-terminally tagged Cse4 yielded estimates ranging from 1 to 8 Cse4 molecules per centromere (Joglekar et al., 2006; Coffman et al., 2011; Lawrimore et al., 2011; Shivaraju et al., 2012; Aravamudhan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Discrepant results for Cse4 stoichiometry can be attributed to inaccuracies in estimating spot intensity in the presence of substantial nuclear background.
source: These discrepant results can be attributed to inaccuracies in estimating spot intensity in the presence of substantial nuclear background, failure to account for the full extent of the centromere cluster (which clearly exceeds the diffraction disk, especially in interphase) in the measurement aperture, or treatment of the cluster as a point source with Gaussian intensity distribution.
evidence: Inferred from analysis of measurement methods.

claim: Bimolecular fluorescence complementation experiments demonstrated that C-terminal Cse4-GFP fusion is deposited on centromeres as a pair during S phase.
source: Interestingly, bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) experiments demonstrated that the C-terminal Cse4-GFP fusion is deposited on centromeres as a pair during S phase, and the fluorescence intensity of a 'lagging' centromere in a dicentric chromosome at anaphase is consistent with the presence of two Cse4-GFP molecules (Aravamudhan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aravamudhan et al., 2013.

claim: Photometry measurements of internally tagged Cse4-GFP support the presence of two molecules of Cse4 in the singular centromeric nucleosome.
source: Our photometry measurements of internally tagged Cse4-GFP—taking into account the dimensions of centromere clusters—also support the presence of two molecules of Cse4 in the singular centromeric nucleosome.
evidence: Demonstrated by photometry measurements in Figure 7.

claim: The Scm3 chaperone persists at centromeres in every stage of the cell cycle.
source: The Scm3 chaperone persists at centromeres in every stage of the cell cycle (Xiao et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xiao et al., 2011.

claim: Scm3 may dissociate stochastically and re-associate onto centromeres through interactions with Ndc10 and AT-rich CEN DNA.
source: Scm3 may dissociate stochastically, and re-associate onto centromeres through interactions with Ndc10 and AT-rich CEN DNA (Xiao et al., 2011; Cho and Harrison, 2011a).
evidence: Speculated based on known interactions and supported by citations.

claim: Dynamic exchange of Scm3 explains the lack of Scm3 in biochemical purifications of kinetochores.
source: This dynamic property explains the lack of Scm3 in biochemical purifications of kinetochores (Westermann et al., 2003; Akiyoshi et al., 2009), its absence as a stable component of reconstituted Cse4 octasome (Dechassa et al., 2011) and fluctuations in measurements of Scm3 occupancy by ChIP (Luconi et al., 2011; Mishra et al., 2011; Shivaraju et al., 2011; Xiao et al., 2011).
evidence: Inferred from Scm3 dynamics and supported by citations.

claim: Biochemical experiments document classic chaperone properties for the conserved Cse4-binding domain of Scm3.
source: Indeed, biochemical experiments document classic chaperone properties for the conserved Cse4-binding domain of Scm3 (Dechassa et al., 2011; Shivaraju et al., 2011; Xiao et al., 2011), and NMR and crystal structures of this domain show that DNA binding by Cse4-H4 in the nucleosome is physically incompatible with continued Scm3 interaction (Zhou et al., 2011; Cho and Harrison, 2011b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DNA binding by Cse4-H4 in the nucleosome is physically incompatible with continued Scm3 interaction.
source: Indeed, biochemical experiments document classic chaperone properties for the conserved Cse4-binding domain of Scm3 (Dechassa et al., 2011; Shivaraju et al., 2011; Xiao et al., 2011), and NMR and crystal structures of this domain show that DNA binding by Cse4-H4 in the nucleosome is physically incompatible with continued Scm3 interaction (Zhou et al., 2011; Cho and Harrison, 2011b).
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Full-length Scm3 is enriched at centromeres through all of the cell cycle stages.
source: However, full-length Scm3 (containing the Ndc10 and DNA binding domains) is enriched at centromeres through all of the cell cycle stages (Xiao et al., 2011), consistent with live cell imaging, and genetic studies suggesting the importance of Scm3 after Cse4 deposition (Camahort et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Steady-state occupancy with dynamic exchange has been described for heterochromatin protein HP1.
source: Steady-state occupancy with dynamic exchange has been described for other chromatin proteins, notably the heterochromatin protein HP1, which functions as a platform for assembling gene silencing complexes (Cheutin et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cheutin et al., 2003.

claim: It is highly likely that Scm3 remains after deposition of Cse4 to safeguard the integrity of the singular centromeric nucleosome.
source: Thus, it is highly likely that Scm3 remains after deposition of Cse4 to safeguard the integrity of the singular centromeric nucleosome on each budding yeast chromosome.
evidence: Inferred from Scm3 dynamics and persistence data.

claim: In G1, a stable Cse4 nucleosome is maintained by steady-state occupancy of Scm3.
source: In G1, a stable Cse4 nucleosome is maintained by steady-state occupancy of Scm3, which would capture and redeposit Cse4-H4 if any stochastic dissociation occurs.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental data.

claim: Early in S phase, centromeric nucleosomes are disrupted, leading to removal and degradation of old Cse4, with kinetochore detachment.
source: Early in S phase, centromeric nucleosomes are disrupted, leading to removal and degradation of old Cse4, with kinetochore detachment (Kitamura et al., 2007).
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental data and supported by citation.

claim: The centromeric nucleosome is re-established in a step-wise process starting with binding of CBF1 to CDEI and CBF3 to CDEIII with assistance of Scm3.
source: The centromeric nucleosome is then re-established in a step-wise process, most likely starting with binding of CBF1 to CDEI, and CBF3 to CDEIII with assistance of Scm3 (Camahort et al., 2007; Mizuguchi et al., 2007).
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: Two Scm3-Cse4-H4 heterotrimers are recruited by Ndc10, the dimeric component of CBF3.
source: Subsequently, two Scm3-Cse4-H4 heterotrimers are recruited by Ndc10, the dimeric component of CBF3 (Cho and Harrison, 2011a).
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental data and supported by citation.

claim: Scm3 deposits each Cse4-H4 on CEN DNA through a dimer intermediate to form a (Cse4-H4)2 tetrasome.
source: Scm3 then deposits each Cse4-H4 on CEN DNA through a dimer intermediate to form a (Cse4-H4)2 tetrasome (Dechassa et al., 2014).
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental data and supported by citation.

claim: During Cse4-H4 deposition, CDEII DNA out-competes Cse4-H4 contacts with Scm3.
source: During this step, CDEII DNA out-competes Cse4-H4 contacts with Scm3, which nonetheless remains in close proximity through interactions with Ndc10 and AT-rich CEN DNA.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental data.

claim: Assembly of two H2A-H2B dimers likely follows formation of the (Cse4-H4)2 tetrasome.
source: Assembly of two H2A-H2B dimers is likely to follow, although their topography may be altered, as indicated by lack of formaldehyde cross-linking (Mizuguchi et al., 2007; Xiao et al., 2011; Krassovsky et al., 2012).
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: The stable state of Cse4-nucleosomes is octameric.
source: Thus, the stable state of Cse4-nucleosomes is octameric, although transient, sub-octameric intermediates may occur during assembly or disassembly.
evidence: Concluded from experimental data.

claim: Transient, sub-octameric intermediates may occur during assembly or disassembly of Cse4 nucleosomes.
source: Thus, the stable state of Cse4-nucleosomes is octameric, although transient, sub-octameric intermediates may occur during assembly or disassembly.
evidence: Speculated based on assembly model.

claim: Scm3 serves as a persistent chaperone-in-residence to insure against catastrophic loss of the singular Cse4 nucleosome.
source: By remaining in close proximity, Scm3 serves not as a structural replacement for H2A-H2B (contrary to our initial model in Mizuguchi et al. (2007)), but rather as a persistent chaperone-in-residence to insure against catastrophic loss of the singular Cse4 nucleosome.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental data.

claim: Fungal Scm3 orthologs possess a diversity of DNA binding motifs.
source: Given that fungal Scm3 orthologs possess a diversity of DNA binding motifs (Aravind et al., 2007), the centromeric persistence of this chaperone through the majority of the Schizosaccharomyces pombe cell cycle (Pidoux et. al, 2009; Williams et al., 2009) or the entirety of the Saccharomyces cerevisiae cell cycle (this study) may be a common theme of CENP-A/CenH3 chaperone function.
evidence: Supported by citations.

claim: The centromeric persistence of Scm3 through the majority of the Schizosaccharomyces pombe cell cycle may be a common theme of CENP-A/CenH3 chaperone function.
source: Given that fungal Scm3 orthologs possess a diversity of DNA binding motifs (Aravind et al., 2007), the centromeric persistence of this chaperone through the majority of the Schizosaccharomyces pombe cell cycle (Pidoux et. al, 2009; Williams et al., 2009) or the entirety of the Saccharomyces cerevisiae cell cycle (this study) may be a common theme of CENP-A/CenH3 chaperone function.
evidence: Speculated based on data from multiple organisms and supported by citations.

claim: The centromeric persistence of Scm3 through the entirety of the Saccharomyces cerevisiae cell cycle may be a common theme of CENP-A/CenH3 chaperone function.
source: Given that fungal Scm3 orthologs possess a diversity of DNA binding motifs (Aravind et al., 2007), the centromeric persistence of this chaperone through the majority of the Schizosaccharomyces pombe cell cycle (Pidoux et. al, 2009; Williams et al., 2009) or the entirety of the Saccharomyces cerevisiae cell cycle (this study) may be a common theme of CENP-A/CenH3 chaperone function.
evidence: Speculated based on data from this study and other organisms.
